extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility (life sciences & data processing)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG) / MPEP procedures to determine whether patent claims recite judicial exceptions and whether additional claim elements integrate those exceptions into a practical application or provide 'significantly more.' Includes life-sciences and data-processing examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation / broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, terms of the claim are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. The same claim interpretation must be used when evaluating the claim for compliance with all requirements (eligibility, definiteness, novelty, non-obviousness, written description, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2111. Practice note: where a wherein clause or other clause provides a patentable distinction in the eligibility analysis, that same interpretation and distinction will apply across other patentability requirements (e.g., prior art applied to 112(f) elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation satisfies the three-prong test set forth in MPEP 2181, it is interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function). When 112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the limitation is limited to the structure, material, or acts (and equivalents) disclosed and clearly linked in the specification to performance of the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should establish the 112(f) interpretation and provide an explanation in the Office action using appropriate form paragraphs. See MPEP 2181 and related sections (2182, 2183) and training (e.g., USPTO CBT on addressing 35 U.S.C. 112(f)). Example: 'means for temperature measuring' limited to the disclosed thermocouple (ARCXY) and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within any statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.03. Example: a claimed 'controller' is a mechanical and/or electrical device (e.g., a general purpose computer with sensors), so the claim is to a manufacture or machine (Step 1: YES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon). A claim 'recites' an exception where the exception is set forth or described in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(II) and 2019 PEG. Example: a limitation that requires 'comparing the obtained temperatures to a target temperature' is an observation/evaluation that falls within the 'mental processes' grouping of abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a practical application / 'other meaningful limitations'
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application. Perform this by (a) identifying any additional elements beyond the judicial exception and (b) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 2019 PEG Section III(A)(2). Additional elements that apply the exception in a particular, technical way (e.g., using comparison output to drive corrective control of machinery to solve a technical problem) can be 'other meaningful limitations' that integrate the exception. Example: a limitation that maintains mold temperature within two degrees and thereby prevents undercure/overcure is a meaningful limitation that integrates the exception and renders the claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (mere data gathering / field-of-use) at Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that merely gather data, provide an environment/field-of-use context, or are recited at a high level of generality may be 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and therefore do not integrate an exception into a practical application at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.05(g),(h). Examples: obtaining temperature measurements (mere data gathering), filling/heating the mold as field-of-use context, presenting offers to collect response statistics. At Step 2A this determination does not take into account whether the limitation is well-understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' / inventive concept analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception — i.e., whether any additional element or combination of elements adds an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.05 and 2019 PEG Section III(B). Under Step 2B, re-evaluate earlier 'insignificant extra-solution activity' determinations while taking into account whether the extra-solution activity is well-known or conventional. Example: use of an unconventional ARCXY thermocouple (not well-known in the claimed field) can elevate an otherwise insignificant data-gathering element into a meaningful inventive concept, making the claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements consideration (technical improvement requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'improvements' consideration requires evaluation of the specification and the claim to ensure a technical explanation of the asserted improvement is present in the specification and that the claim reflects the asserted improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement except when a person of ordinary skill, consulting the claims and specification, would clearly understand the invention does not improve technology as applicant asserts. Under the 2019 PEG, examiners should perform the improvements analysis at Step 2A Prong Two without reference to what is well-understood, routine, or conventional. See FAQ G-2, MPEP 2106.05(a), and Advanced Module training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception / physicality not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere instructions to apply a judicial exception (e.g., 'apply it' via a controller) cannot supply an inventive concept, and mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not a relevant consideration in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.05(I) and Alice (573 U.S. 208). A generic controller that only instructs to apply an abstract idea does not integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use limitations are generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate the field of use or technological environment in which an exception is performed (e.g., administering a drug, using a controller in injection molding) are treated as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.05(h). Such field-of-use/context elements typically do not integrate the exception into a practical application unless they contribute a meaningful, technical improvement beyond mere context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider combination of additional elements (can change outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are insignificant by themselves, their combination should be evaluated to determine whether together they integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 2019 PEG Section III(A)(2). The analysis requires assessing both individual elements and the elements in combination; in some examples, combinations of meaningful limitations produce eligibility even if some individual elements are data-gathering or field-of-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not consider conventionality at Step 2A when evaluating 'insignificant extra-solution activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity at Step 2A (Prong Two), the analysis should not take into account whether the element is well-understood, routine, or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, conventionality is considered at Step 2B when determining whether the claim amounts to significantly more. See 2019 PEG guidance and MPEP 2106.05(g).
